name: write-ahead-log
context: State that must survive a crash is written to a durable, ordered log before it is considered committed, and recovery replays that log. The local store is a cache: in Kafka Streams the compacted changelog topic is the source of truth and RocksDB is only a non-fault-tolerant lookup structure whose flush timing is uncontrolled. Under exactly-once processing the log write, the input offset commit and the output write must be atomic — and because local store writes were historically not atomic with the changelog commit, a crash would wipe the entire store and replay the changelog, with observed stalls spanning multiple days for high-cardinality tables.
benefits: Recovery is a replay from a known offset rather than a checkpoint of the whole working set
Makes the durability boundary explicit and auditable — the log is the record of what happened
Enables end-to-end exactly-once by committing offsets, changelog and output atomically
Turns state changes into a stream that can be compacted, replicated, audited or fed to other consumers
Bounds recovery cost by commit interval and log length rather than by the size of the working set
tradeoffs: Write amplification: every state change is written locally and to the log, so throughput and storage cost roughly double
Non-windowed state only compacts; windowed keys carry the window in the key, so compaction can never purge old entries and the log grows until retention
Transactional state stores buffer uncommitted writes in memory, so a generous commit interval can push meaningful memory pressure
Finer-grained logging makes checkpoints faster and more stable but increases recovery replay time and space use
A log is an operational liability: retention, segment counts and rebalance interaction must all be managed
use_cases: Stream processing state that must be restored exactly after a task or machine failure
Exactly-once pipelines writing to Kafka topics and to transactional external sinks
Local state stores backed by RocksDB, where the changelog is authoritative and the store is a cache
Incremental checkpointing systems that log state deltas and materialise full snapshots in the background
Audit-grade pipelines where the log of state changes doubles as the compliance record
avoid_when: The workload is stateless — there is nothing to make durable beyond the log you already write
The log would be retained forever and compaction cannot apply, making storage unbounded for no benefit
The sink cannot participate in the transaction, so the exactly-once claim is not actually achievable
Recovery from a full recomputation is cheaper than maintaining a log
component_types: Changelog topic: compacted, durable ordered log of state changes; the authoritative copy
Local state store: RocksDB or in-memory cache used for lookups, rebuildable from the changelog
Commit protocol: periodic flush of stores plus offset commit, or a transaction spanning both
Transactional state store: buffers writes until the corresponding changelog transaction commits
Position/checkpoint file: maps local store contents to changelog offsets so recovery knows what is valid
Restore procedure: replays the changelog to reconstruct the store after a task moves machines
technology_stack: Apache Flink (changelog state backend, incremental checkpoints)
anti_patterns: Treating the local RocksDB cache as the durable copy and configuring no changelog at all
Assuming exactly-once makes local state crash-safe: without transactional state stores a crash still wipes and replays
Leaving changelog replication at its default of one, losing fault tolerance exactly when the state matters
Retaining windowed changelogs indefinitely, since (key, window) keys defeat compaction entirely
Setting commit intervals so large that transactional buffering exhausts heap on high-cardinality stores
design_principles: Log first, cache second — the cache is derived and may be discarded
Commit atomically or do not claim exactly-once
Recovery cost is a function of commit interval and log length, both of which are design parameters
Windowed state needs explicit retention because compaction cannot help it
The log's retention policy is part of the design, not an afterthought
best_practices: Enable transactional state stores so a crash replays only uncommitted records instead of wiping the store
Name state stores and their changelog topics explicitly so topology evolution does not orphan recovery data
Bound uncommitted-write buffering with an explicit byte threshold rather than relying on the commit interval alone
Set changelog replication above one and monitor restore time, not just task liveness
Test recovery by killing tasks on different machines, and measure how long restore actually takes
references: Matthias Sax, Kafka Streams Internal Data Management — changelog topic is the source of truth, RocksDB is a non-fault-tolerant cache, https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=65864917
KIP-844: Transactional State Stores — crash failure wipes and replays state today; atomic commit proposal, https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-844%3A+Transactional+State+Stores

Apache Flink, Improving speed and stability of checkpointing with generic log-based incremental checkpoints, https://flink.apache.org/2022/05/30/improving-speed-and-stability-of-checkpointing-with-generic-log-based-incremental-checkpoints/
Apache Kafka, Core Concepts — processing guarantees and exactly-once (KIP-129, KIP-447), https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/
Apache Kafka, Streams Architecture — fault tolerance and recovery, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/architecture/
